title: Kerberos Password-Spray Pre-Authentication Failures
exclusions: This rule detects one source address producing Microsoft Security Event ID 4771 with exact failure code `0x18` for more than 30 distinct non-computer account names in one closed five-minute bucket. Because the comparison is strict, the minimum trigger is 31 distinct accounts. It does not alert on 30 or fewer accounts, repeated guessing against one account, machine accounts ending in `$`, low-and-slow attempts spread across buckets or source addresses, successful authentication, NTLM failures, Kerberos service-ticket failures, malformed requests that do not generate 4771, accounts configured not to require Kerberos pre-authentication, or telemetry absent from a domain controller. Codes `0x6` (unknown client principal), `0x10` (unsupported pre-authentication data type), `0x12` (client credentials revoked), `0x17` (key/password expired), and `0x25` (clock skew too great) require separate operational or security rules and are intentionally excluded. A result does not prove that the source is hostile, that all account names are valid, or that any password was accepted. The catalogue SPL applies no exception lookup and makes no runtime, attribution, prevention, or regulatory-assurance claim.
evidence: After deployment, retain the version-controlled `windows_kerberos_password_spray_4771` saved-search definition and ACL; schedule, dispatch, and triggered-alert history; every result row with five-minute bucket, normalized source address, failure count, distinct-account denominator, target users/SIDs, domain controllers, service, pre-authentication types, ticket options, source ports, exact `0x18` code, source, and source type; the corresponding raw 4771 XML/EventRecordIDs from each domain controller; effective Advanced Audit Policy evidence; effective WinEventLog input and Splunk Add-on for Microsoft Windows version; domain-controller/source-health results; dated positive and boundary-negative control outputs; threshold approval; alert delivery; analyst disposition; and any bounded notification exception. This documentation-only review produced no Windows event, Splunk search job, authentication attempt, alert, or production evidence.

controlTest.positiveScenario: In an isolated test index, place 31 XML Security events inside the same fixed five-minute bucket. Every event has `source=XmlWinEventLog:Security`, `sourcetype=XmlWinEventLog`, `EventCode=4771`, `Computer=DC01.example`, `IpAddress=::ffff:10.0.0.50`, `Status=0x18`, `ServiceName=krbtgt/EXAMPLE`, `PreAuthType=2`, and a different `TargetUserName` from `spray-user-01` through `spray-user-31`; none ends in `$`. Expect exactly one row with `src_ip=10.0.0.50`, `failure_count=31`, `unique_accounts=31`, `failure_code=0x18`, and `failure_reason=KDC_ERR_PREAUTH_FAILED: invalid pre-authentication data (commonly wrong password)`. Repeat one event with uppercase `0X18` and confirm normalization without changing the distinct count. Documentation review checks the expected logic but does not claim replay.
controlTest.negativeScenario: Run isolated variants and expect zero rows for each: exactly 30 distinct non-computer users from one address in one bucket; 31 failures for one user; 31 distinct names ending in `$`; 31 distinct users with Status `0x6`; 31 distinct users split across two source addresses with neither source above 30; 31 distinct users split across adjacent five-minute buckets with neither bucket above 30; qualifying events only in the newest excluded five minutes; and 31 otherwise qualifying events with an empty `IpAddress`. Also duplicate one username with different letter case and confirm it contributes one normalized distinct account, not two.

dataSources: Windows Security Event ID 4771 (`Kerberos pre-authentication failed`) generated only on Active Directory domain controllers when the Key Distribution Center cannot issue a Ticket-Granting Ticket after pre-authentication. Enable Failure auditing for **Account Logon > Audit Kerberos Authentication Service**. Collect the Security channel directly in XML with Splunk Add-on for Microsoft Windows (Splunkbase 742) into the deployment-local `wineventlog` index. The primary supported contract is `sourcetype=XmlWinEventLog`, `source=XmlWinEventLog:Security`. Required XML/TA fields are `EventCode`/`EventID`, `Computer`, `TargetUserName`, `TargetSid`, `ServiceName`, `TicketOptions`, `Status`, `PreAuthType`, `IpAddress`, and `IpPort`; Microsoft documents certificate fields as empty for 4771. `dest` and `host` are domain-controller fallbacks. Event volume is high on domain controllers; WEF/WEC requires separately validated original-computer identity and latency.
app: Splunk Add-on for Microsoft Windows (`Splunk_TA_windows`, Splunkbase 742), version 10.0.1, installed for Security-channel collection and on the parsing/search tiers required by the deployment. Splunkbase lists 10.0.1 for Splunk Enterprise 9.3 through current 10.x releases and Splunk Cloud at review time. Test upgrades, especially from releases before the documented 5.0.0 breaking-change boundary. No premium app is required; Splunk Enterprise Security can optionally turn the result into a finding.
spl:
index=wineventlog sourcetype="XmlWinEventLog" source="XmlWinEventLog:Security" EventCode=4771 earliest=-10m@m latest=-5m@m
| eval event_code=tonumber(coalesce(EventCode,EventID)), failure_code=lower(trim(Status)), target_user=lower(trim(TargetUserName)), src_ip=lower(replace(trim(IpAddress),"^::ffff:","")), domain_controller=lower(trim(coalesce(dest,Computer,host)))
| where event_code=4771 AND failure_code="0x18" AND len(target_user)>0 AND NOT like(target_user,"%$") AND len(src_ip)>0 AND len(domain_controller)>0
| bin _time span=5m
| stats count as failure_count dc(target_user) as unique_accounts values(target_user) as target_users values(TargetSid) as target_sids values(domain_controller) as domain_controllers values(ServiceName) as services values(PreAuthType) as preauth_types values(TicketOptions) as ticket_options values(IpPort) as source_ports values(source) as observed_sources values(sourcetype) as observed_sourcetypes by _time src_ip failure_code
| where unique_accounts>30
| eval failure_reason="KDC_ERR_PREAUTH_FAILED: invalid pre-authentication data (commonly wrong password)", detection_pattern="more than 30 distinct non-computer accounts from one source in one closed five-minute bucket"
| rename _time as bucket_start
| table bucket_start src_ip failure_code failure_reason failure_count unique_accounts target_users target_sids domain_controllers services preauth_types ticket_options source_ports observed_sources observed_sourcetypes detection_pattern
| sort 0 -unique_accounts -failure_count src_ip
description: Reports a source address when a closed five-minute bucket contains Security Event ID 4771 failure code `0x18` for at least 31 distinct non-computer account names. The row preserves the exact unique-account denominator, total failures, accounts, domain controllers, service, ticket options, and pre-authentication types used to assess a possible Kerberos password spray.
value: Password spraying deliberately spreads guesses across many accounts to reduce per-account lockout signals. Detecting the pattern at the domain controllers can expose an attempt before a valid credential is found and reused, while the source/account evidence helps identity and incident-response teams contain the origin, protect targeted users, and avoid indiscriminate lockouts.
implementation: Enable Failure auditing for `Audit Kerberos Authentication Service` on every domain controller, collect the Security channel as XML, and validate the native 4771 fields before alerting. Save the SPL as `windows_kerberos_password_spray_4771`, run it every five minutes over the preceding delayed closed bucket, and trigger on any row. The starting policy follows Splunk Security Content's strict `unique_accounts > 30` rule—31 is the first triggering value—and scopes to Microsoft-documented `Status=0x18`; tune only after boundary tests and fleet-specific review.
visualization: On a restricted Active Directory authentication dashboard, put domain-controller Security-source health first. Add a single value for spray sources over 24 hours; a five-minute timechart of `unique_accounts` and `failure_count` by `src_ip` with a reference line at 30; a bar chart of top source addresses; and a result table with bucket, source, domain controllers, distinct accounts, total failures, target users, pre-authentication types, and ticket options. Row drilldown should open exact raw 4771 events plus subsequent 4768 successes and relevant 4624 logons for the same accounts/source, without asserting causal success.
schema: Microsoft-Windows-Security-Auditing Event ID 4771 native XML fields parsed by Splunk Add-on for Microsoft Windows
dataModelAcceleration: No accelerated CIM substitute is claimed. Splunk's current Windows add-on field-mapping documentation lists Event ID 4771 with fields such as `Error_Code`, `category`, `service`, `service_name`, `ta_windows_action`, and `vendor_product`, but does not document a 4771 mapping that preserves native `IpAddress`, `TargetUserName`, exact `Status`, and the five-minute distinct-account denominator in the Authentication data model. A generic `Authentication.action=failure` tstats search mixes protocols/events and cannot reproduce this rule. At scale, summarize the exact raw 4771 dimensions only after parity and completeness tests.

knownFalsePositives:
A result contains genuine `0x18` pre-authentication failures for at least 31 normalized account names. “False positive” means the concentration has an authorized or non-adversarial cause, not that the KDC records are false.

1. **Citrix Virtual Apps and Desktops or Microsoft Remote Desktop Session Host credential pass-through fault** — A shared broker/session host can be the visible Kerberos source for many users after a policy, StoreFront, profile, or credential-provider change. Confirm the source IP in CMDB, exact maintenance/change record, Citrix/RDS authentication logs, affected session population, onset, and recovery. Do not suppress all traffic from the server; use an expiring exception for the exact source and incident window while the identity fault is repaired.

2. **Tenable, Qualys, or Rapid7 credentialed assessment node** — A mis-scoped password audit or credentialed scan can try many configured accounts from one scanner. Verify scanner ownership, job ID, approved targets, stored credential set, UTC run window, and scan-console evidence. Disable or correct the job rather than permanently allowlisting the scanner; if a notification exception is necessary, bind it to the scanner IP, job/change ID, and short validity period.

3. **Load, failover, or migration test for an application that centrally requests Kerberos tickets** — A JMeter/custom harness, VDI migration, identity-provider cutover, or disaster-recovery exercise can replay many intentionally invalid test accounts through one source. Require nonproduction account prefixes, an approved test plan, isolated assets, exact source, operator, and UTC bounds. Keep the detection as control evidence and suppress duplicate paging only for that test window.

4. **Atomic Red Team, purple-team, or penetration-test password spray** — An authorized T1110.003 simulation should trigger. Correlate the source address, operator, engagement ID, approved target account set, rate, and timebox. Preserve the alert and raw events as test evidence; apply only a post-detection, expiring notification exception after confirming the engagement.

5. **Shared authentication middleware after a broad password reset or stale credential-cache event** — A documented enterprise access gateway or application tier can retry many users through one Kerberos client identity/source after a credential migration. Prove the architecture and incident with application logs, change ticket, account-owner reports, and cessation after cache/configuration repair. A source-wide permanent allowlist would create a blind spot if that middleware is later compromised.

**Safe suppression:** preserve the base result and source-health evidence. Apply any alert-wrapper lookup only after aggregation, keyed by exact `src_ip,exception_id` with owner, approver, reason, numeric `valid_from_epoch`, and exclusive `valid_until_epoch`. Reject wildcards and open-ended rows. Never suppress because the source is internal, a domain controller is busy, or an account list contains expected users.
hardware: Supported Active Directory domain controllers generating Security Event ID 4771. Member servers and workstations are clients/source addresses, not the systems on which Microsoft documents this event as generated. Direct domain-controller collection is the primary contract; WEF/WEC requires validated original-computer fields, latency, and capacity.

cost.search_load_notes: The five-minute search is narrow and aggregate-only, but the Security channel and Kerberos Authentication Service audit subcategory can be high volume on domain controllers. Keep index/source/Event ID predicates and size collection from measured DC traffic.

detailedImplementation:
## Prerequisites and exact detection contract

Assign an Active Directory owner, Windows audit-policy owner, Splunk collection owner, SOC detection owner, identity incident responder, and exception approver. Inventory every writable and read-only domain controller in scope and its Security-log collection path. Install a currently supported Splunk Add-on for Microsoft Windows (`Splunk_TA_windows`, Splunkbase 742) release on the collection tier and make its parsing/search knowledge available to the tiers required by the topology. Version 10.0.1 is the current reviewed release and Splunkbase lists support for platform 9.3 through current 10.x releases and Splunk Cloud; qualify the exact Windows Server, forwarder, add-on, CIM, and Splunk versions before production. Follow Splunk's upgrade instructions when crossing the add-on 5.0.0 boundary.

The collection identity must be able to read each domain controller's Security channel. The search role needs read access to the deployment-local `wineventlog` index and permission to save/schedule the alert. Restrict raw records because target account names, SIDs, client addresses, certificate context, and authentication patterns are security-sensitive. Do not grant domain administration, account reset, GPO edit, lookup write, or network-blocking permission merely to execute this search.

Microsoft defines Event ID 4771 as **Kerberos pre-authentication failed**: it is generated only on domain controllers when the KDC fails to issue a TGT after pre-authentication, and it is not generated when the account has **Do not require Kerberos preauthentication** set. It is different from 4768 TGT request results, 4772 TGT request failure, 4769 service-ticket activity, 4625 logon failure, and 4776 NTLM credential validation. Do not combine those IDs under one denominator without a separate design.

The alert's code is exactly `0x18`, `KDC_ERR_PREAUTH_FAILED`: Microsoft describes invalid pre-authentication information and identifies wrong password as a possible/common cause. Do not reuse 4625 NTSTATUS meanings. Other useful Kerberos codes are `0x6` client principal unknown; `0x10` unsupported pre-authentication data type, with Microsoft noting smart-card certificate/DC certificate causes; `0x12` client credentials revoked; `0x17` key expired/password expired; `0x19` additional pre-authentication required; and `0x25` clock skew too great. They represent different conditions and are excluded from this spray alert.

Pre-authentication type is a separate field, not a failure code: Microsoft lists `2` as PA-ENC-TIMESTAMP for standard password authentication, `15`/`16`/`17` for smart-card PKINIT-related exchanges, and `138` for Kerberos armoring/FAST. Preserve it for triage. The rule normalizes account names to lowercase because Active Directory names are case-insensitive for this analytic and excludes names ending `$` because Microsoft documents that suffix for computer accounts.

The aggregation follows Splunk Security Content: one source, one five-minute bucket, `Status=0x18`, non-computer accounts, and strict `unique_accounts > 30`. That means 31 distinct normalized names is the minimum result—not 30, not six failures per user, and not “more than ten failures per user.” Repeated attempts against one account are password guessing and need another rule. The threshold is a starting content policy, not a Microsoft limit; low-and-slow adversaries can stay below it.

## Step 1 — Enable auditing and collect domain-controller Security XML

Apply Advanced Audit Policy through a domain-controller GPO at **Computer Configuration > Policies > Windows Settings > Security Settings > Advanced Audit Policy Configuration > Audit Policies > Account Logon > Audit Kerberos Authentication Service**. Enable **Failure**; enable Success separately if required for broader 4768 visibility. On a canary DC verify effective policy rather than assuming GPO application:

```cmd
auditpol /get /subcategory:"Kerberos Authentication Service"
```

Use Resultant Set of Policy or `gpresult` to identify the winning GPO. Microsoft warns that this subcategory is high volume on KDCs. Measure Security records/day and bytes/day per DC before changing retention or forwarding architecture. Monitor policy-change events and effective-policy drift separately.

For direct collection, manage the local input outside the add-on's `default` directory:

```ini
[WinEventLog://Security]
disabled = 0
renderXml = true
index = wineventlog
checkpointInterval = 5
```

`wineventlog` is a deployment-local catalogue choice, not a vendor default. Add-on 6.0.0 and later renders WinEventLog XML by default, producing `sourcetype=XmlWinEventLog` with `source=XmlWinEventLog:Security`; keep `renderXml=true` explicit in the governed app. Record checkpoint/start settings and any XPath allow/deny filter. Filtering out 4771 destroys this control. Use TLS-protected forwarding and size queues and native Security-log retention for outage/backlog conditions.

WEF/WEC can collect the same events, but it is not interchangeable without tests. Preserve original `Computer`, avoid duplicate direct plus forwarded collection, measure event-time-to-index-time latency, and ensure the subscription query includes 4771. A collector's `host` must not replace the originating DC. At high DC volume, capacity-test subscriptions and collectors before cutover.

Verify native fields against Microsoft Event XML:

```spl
index=wineventlog sourcetype="XmlWinEventLog" source="XmlWinEventLog:Security" EventCode=4771 earliest=-24h
| table _time Computer EventRecordID TargetUserName TargetSid ServiceName TicketOptions Status PreAuthType IpAddress IpPort CertIssuerName CertSerialNumber CertThumbprint
| head 20
```

Require correct DC identity and populated target user, service, status, source address, and event record identity. Microsoft documents certificate issuer, serial, and thumbprint as always empty in 4771; do not invent certificate values or use their emptiness as a parser-failure signal. Validate event counts and records against Event Viewer **Windows Logs > Security** on two DCs over fixed UTC bounds. Establish separate source-health coverage for every expected DC.

## Step 2 — Create and understand the spray search

Save the primary SPL as `windows_kerberos_password_spray_4771`. Schedule it every five minutes, for example `*/5 * * * *`, and trigger when result count is greater than zero. It evaluates the nonoverlapping bucket from ten to five minutes before the schedule boundary. Five minutes of close delay is only a starting allowance; measure `_indextime-_time` p95/p99 and increase the delay if needed while preserving nonoverlapping event-time buckets.

The base search constrains the local index, XML source type, exact Security source, and Event ID. `event_code` accepts the add-on's `EventCode` and native `EventID`; no unrelated IDs are admitted. Lowercasing `Status` permits case variation while retaining the exact hexadecimal text. `IpAddress` normalization strips only Microsoft's documented IPv4-mapped IPv6 prefix `::ffff:`; it retains native IPv6 and `::1`. Do not treat an internal or loopback source as benign by default.

Account names are trimmed and lowercased before `dc()`. Computer accounts ending `$` are removed before both numerator and denominator. `bin` fixes the five-minute bucket, and `stats` counts every admitted failure while independently counting distinct accounts. Multiple failures for one account increase `failure_count` but not `unique_accounts`. Grouping by source address—not DC—allows the same source observed by multiple DCs to form one forest/domain-wide signal, while `domain_controllers` preserves where events were recorded.

The strict final predicate `unique_accounts>30` is deliberately visible. The output includes target accounts/SIDs, DCs, service, pre-authentication types, ticket options, and source ports for triage. Large multi-value account lists can be truncated by UI limits; the numeric denominator remains authoritative, and raw-event drilldown must be retained. Do not reduce the threshold merely to increase alert count without replaying normal Citrix/RDS, scanner, migration, test, and shared-authentication traffic.

No blanket source allowlist belongs in the base SPL. A known scanner, Citrix host, access gateway, or test system can be compromised or misconfigured. If paging needs suppression, apply the bounded lookup described in `knownFalsePositives` after this result and continue displaying and retaining the base row.

No CIM `tstats` block is supplied. Generic Authentication failures can combine 4625, cloud identity, VPN, NTLM, and other protocols and may not retain `Status`, native source address, target account, or exact event identity. A summary-index implementation must write one row per five-minute `src_ip,target_user,failure_code,domain_controller` with raw counts and completeness markers, then prove parity with raw 4771 events before replacing this search.

## Step 3 — Validate fields, status semantics, threshold, and windows

Execute the positive control in an isolated index with fixed bounds. Generate 31 different non-computer names, not 31 copies of one event. Assert exactly one row and every documented output: normalized IPv4 address, code/reason, `failure_count=31`, `unique_accounts=31`, 31 account names, DC identity, service, pre-auth type, ticket options, source metadata, and bucket start. Test mixed `0x18`/`0X18`; test the `::ffff:` prefix and native IPv6 independently.

Run each negative control separately. Boundary-test 30 versus 31 distinct users. Test duplicate and case-variant names so the denominator cannot be inflated. Test `$` exclusion before aggregation. Test code `0x6`, `0x10`, `0x12`, `0x17`, and `0x25` and confirm none enters this rule; separately verify a diagnostic search decodes them according to Microsoft/RFC semantics. Split attempts across sources and across adjacent buckets. Test events exactly at earliest and latest boundaries; Splunk's latest bound is exclusive. Test missing user, address, and DC identity.

Compare two real or safely generated lab failures with Event Viewer XML. Verify TargetUserName, TargetSid, ServiceName, TicketOptions, Status, PreAuthType, IpAddress, IpPort, Computer, EventRecordID, and UTC timestamp. Use a dedicated lab domain/account and approved test; do not spray production accounts or risk lockout. Verify that successful correction produces expected success telemetry in the broader authentication workflow, but do not require a success event for this alert to fire.

Check collection completeness across all expected DCs over 24 hours, allowing that some DCs may be quiet depending on site/client routing. Reconcile with DC inventory, forwarder health, Security-channel freshness, GPO application, and KDC role. Detect direct/WEF duplicates by Computer, EventRecordID, and timestamp. Record Windows/add-on/forwarder/Splunk versions, GPO and input revisions, fixture generator, exact bounds, expected and actual rows, search job ID, and operator. Keep `status=draft` until runtime controls, source health, threshold replay, alert delivery, dashboard RBAC, and response are accepted by human owners.

## Step 4 — Operationalize triage, response, dashboards, and evidence

Build the dashboard described in `visualization`, placing missing/stale DC feeds above spray results. Restrict account lists and raw Security records to identity/SOC roles. Give service-desk viewers aggregate counts unless they need account-level data. Drill down from the result to exact raw 4771 events, then inspect adjacent 4768 TGT activity and 4624 logons for the same users/source only as correlation; a later success does not automatically prove that the spray obtained that password.

When a result fires: (1) verify source freshness, bucket, raw events, code, distinct denominator, account list, DC identity, and duplicate collection; (2) resolve `src_ip` through DHCP/VPN/NAT/asset records valid at event time; (3) identify scanner, Citrix/RDS, identity middleware, application, or test ownership; (4) search for subsequent successful authentication and privileged-account targeting; (5) contact the identity/SOC owner and preserve evidence; (6) if maliciousness is plausible, contain the source through approved network/EDR controls and apply scoped account protection/reset decisions; and (7) document disposition and tuning feedback.

Do not automatically disable 31 accounts, block a shared NAT/proxy, reset all passwords, stop the KDC, clear Security logs, change lockout policy, or suppress an internal source solely from this result. Broad automated response can create denial of service and erase context. Prioritize high-value or subsequently successful accounts, but use the organization's identity incident process.

Retain the artifacts named in `evidence` under security/privacy policy. Review the threshold after topology changes, Citrix/RDS or scanner deployments, authentication middleware changes, domain migrations, audit-policy/add-on upgrades, and red-team exercises. Maintain companion views for per-account guessing, low-and-slow baselines, unknown-principal `0x6`, smart-card/PADATA `0x10`, expired key `0x17`, and clock skew `0x25`; this UC is intentionally not a universal Kerberos-health rule.

## Step 5 — Troubleshoot Windows, Kerberos, and Splunk failure modes

- **No 4771 events on a DC:** verify it is a domain controller/KDC, effective `Kerberos Authentication Service` Failure auditing, Security-channel input, collection permissions, index routing, and source health. Member servers/workstations do not generate this event under Microsoft's contract.
- **4771 exists in Event Viewer but not Splunk:** inspect effective `[WinEventLog://Security]`, XPath filters, checkpoint state, forwarder queues/outputs, index permissions, and direct versus WEF routing. Compare fixed EventRecordIDs rather than broad counts.
- **Wrong source/source type:** confirm XML rendering and add-on version. Modern XML uses `sourcetype=XmlWinEventLog` and `source=XmlWinEventLog:Security`, not `WinEventLog:Security` as the XML source type.
- **Target/status/IP fields are null:** inspect raw XML Data names and confirm add-on parsing/search-time knowledge on the required tiers. Do not substitute `Account_Name`, 4625 `Status`, or `Source_Network_Address`; those belong to different event contracts.
- **All events appear from the WEC collector:** original Computer/source identity is not preserved or extracted. Repair the WEF subscription/add-on topology before alerting; grouping by collector hides DC coverage and can distort evidence.
- **Expected spray produces no row:** check exact Event ID, `Status=0x18`, machine-account suffix, normalized source, bucket boundary, and distinct—not total—account count. Exactly 30 does not pass `>30`; one user repeated 31 times is not spraying under this rule.
- **Unexpected result from a shared server:** resolve the source at event time, inspect Citrix/RDS/scanner/application logs, account list, pre-auth type, service, and change/test records. Use a bounded post-alert exception only after proving the cause.
- **Large account list is truncated:** rely on `unique_accounts` for the denominator and drill into raw events for the complete set. Review Splunk multi-value/UI limits; do not infer that a truncated display means fewer events.
- **Events arrive in the wrong bucket or late:** compare event UTC time, `_indextime`, DC time service, forwarder queues, WEF latency, and scheduler execution. Increase close delay from measured latency and rerun boundary controls; `0x25` itself is clock-skew telemetry but is excluded from this alert.
- **Duplicate counts across DC/direct/WEF paths:** compare Computer, EventRecordID, `_time`, source, and forwarder. Correct topology and backfill clean baseline evidence rather than raising the threshold.
- **Search cost or Security ingest is high:** retain index/source/Event ID predicates, review DC audit volume and filters, and consider a governed 4771 summary with parity checks. Do not disable Kerberos Failure auditing or discard `0x18` at index time merely to make the search cheaper.
grandmaExplanation: We notice when one computer tries a bad password against many different accounts in a few minutes. That pattern can reveal someone quietly testing a common password before they find an account that lets them in.
